title: Uniform and Regiment
premise: In 1917, Freya Quintana keeps a field hospital ledger in which she records the names of soldiers the officers' reports omit—the unlettered, the colonial troops, the deserters. When a stranger arrives bearing letters written in the unmistakable hand of her brother Edmund, officially dead at Ypres two years prior, Freya's careful invisibility shatters: Edmund is alive, court-martialed for desertion, and scheduled for execution unless a family member claims him before transport leaves. But there is only one berth on the last ambulance south, and Freya must choose between claiming her brother and evacuating Tomas, a wounded colonial orderly whose name exists only because she wrote it down. She gives the berth to Tomas, then walks to the court-martial herself and testifies that the ledger—her ledger of the omitted—is proof enough of who deserves saving. Edmund is spared by commutation; Freya finally accepts that history has been happening to her all along.
about_author: Beatrix Oyelaran is a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing regimental hospital records from the First World War. She writes historical fiction about the people official paperwork tried to erase.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Omissions
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. In a dressing station near Arras, Freya tends wounds by day and secretly records omitted names by night—Tomas among them. Officers praise her discretion. Emotional beat: the quiet pride of an invisible woman who believes history happens elsewhere, to other people.

chapters.title: Names Not Written
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. A colonel demands her ledger for inspection; she shows him a falsified copy while the true one hides in her boot. Tomas notices her trembling hands and says nothing. Emotional beat: first crack in her belief that staying invisible is safe—or possible.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Gate
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. During a bombardment, a mud-caked stranger arrives asking for 'the Quintana girl' and produces letters in Edmund's unmistakable handwriting. He claims her brother is alive at a disciplinary camp. Emotional beat: vertigo—the dead writing letters, the past refusing burial.

chapters.title: What Edmund Left Behind
chapters.summary: Freya, POV, with flashback. She rereads Edmund's last pre-Ypres letter and their childhood promise never to abandon each other. The stranger, Callum, explains Edmund deserted after shell shock and faces execution. Emotional beat: grief reopening like a wound she'd stitched shut.

chapters.title: The Berth
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. Matron announces one berth on the final ambulance south before the line collapses—priority given to documented patients. Freya realizes documentation is power, and she holds the only pen. Emotional beat: dawning, terrible agency.

chapters.title: Tomas's Fever
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. Delirious with gangrene fever, Tomas dreams of Lagos and his mother, unaware he is dying or that a nurse writes his name nightly. Emotional beat: tenderness toward a man who doesn't know he exists on paper.

chapters.title: Callum's Bargain
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. Callum reveals he was Edmund's comrade and owes him a life debt; he pressures Freya to claim her brother within four days or lose him forever. Emotional beat: resentment at being forced from the margins into a decision.

chapters.title: Blood and Ink
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. She drafts a claim letter for Edmund, then visits Tomas's cot and finds his real name spoken aloud for the first time by his own lips. Emotional beat: the ledger stops being ink and becomes flesh.

chapters.title: The Colonel's Daughter
chapters.summary: Colonel Ashworth, POV. The colonel, whose daughter died serving as a VAD, suspects Freya's ledger is irregular and begins pulling her service file. Emotional beat: menace from the machinery of record-keeping turned against its keeper.

chapters.title: Inheritance of Silence
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. A letter from home reveals their father hid Edmund's shell-shock diagnosis years ago, choosing reputation over son. Freya sees her own invisibility as inherited. Emotional beat: fury at the family habit of erasure.

chapters.title: Forty-Eight Hours
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. The ambulance departure moves up; Callum warns the execution order will not wait. Freya works through the night deciding, writing and burning draft after draft. Emotional beat: claustrophobic pressure as time collapses.

chapters.title: What Tomas Carried
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. Semi-lucid, Tomas tells Freya about the men in his unit whose deaths were never reported—'we are not missing, we are unwritten.' He asks only that someone remember. Emotional beat: the weight of being asked to be remembered.

chapters.title: The Falsified Page
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. Desperate, Freya considers forging Tomas's transfer papers onto the ambulance list—a crime that would end her. Matron catches her with the pen hovering. Emotional beat: shame and the seduction of becoming what she despises.

chapters.title: Matron's War
chapters.summary: Matron Hale, POV. Hale recalls losing her own brother to an unrecorded grave and quietly covers Freya's near-forgery, revealing she has known about the ledger for months. Emotional beat: unexpected sisterhood across rank.

chapters.title: Ashworth's File
chapters.summary: Colonel Ashworth, POV. Ashworth finds discrepancies between Freya's ledgers and confronts her privately, offering protection in exchange for her silence about the omitted colonial casualties. Emotional beat: corruption dressed as mercy; the trap closing.

chapters.title: The Choice
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. Dawn of departure day. Freya signs the berth to Tomas and sends Callum alone to Edmund with her testimony instead of her claim. Emotional beat: agonizing release—choosing the many unnamed over the one beloved.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. She travels under Red Cross papers to the court-martial and reads her ledger aloud as evidence that Edmund's desertion followed untreated shell shock the army itself failed to record. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into voice; invisibility weaponized.

chapters.title: Verdict and Veto
chapters.summary: Edmund, POV. Shackled, Edmund hears his sister's voice through the wall and learns their father's old concealment is exposed. The sentence is commuted to a medical discharge. Emotional beat: shattered man receiving an inheritance he never wanted—being seen.

chapters.title: Reckoning
chapters.summary: Colonel Ashworth, POV. Ashworth attempts to bury the ledger testimony but finds Matron Hale has already mailed copies to three newspapers. His career fractures. Emotional beat: the machinery of omission devouring its own officer.

chapters.title: The Last Ambulance South
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. At the railhead, Tomas boards, lucid at last, and presses his dog tag into her hand: 'Write it where they can't burn it.' The train pulls out. Emotional beat: bittersweet severance and purpose confirmed.

chapters.title: Brother, Sister, Stranger
chapters.summary: Freya and Edmund, alternating POV. Reunited at the camp gate, they grieve the years and the lie between them without absolving their father. Edmund asks to read every page of her ledger. Emotional beat: reconciliation built on truth rather than blood alone.

chapters.title: Uniform and Regiment
chapters.summary: Freya, POV, epilogue 1919. In London, Freya publishes the ledger as a memorial roll; Tomas's name appears in print beside hundreds of others. Edmund plants a garden. Emotional beat: belonging claimed at last—history happened to her, and now it belongs to everyone she named.
